description: Build a personal knowledge management system (second brain) using the capture, organize, distill, express architecture. The system is append-only at capture time, searchable instead of perfectly organized, and project-oriented instead of topic-oriented.

steps.description: Inventory every channel where information enters your life (email, chat, meetings, reading, conversations, browsing, podcasts) and set up a frictionless capture path from each one into a single inbox.

inputs.name: current-information-sources
inputs.desc: List of all places where you currently encounter information worth keeping

inputs.name: current-note-tools
inputs.desc: Note-taking and storage tools you already use

outputs.name: capture-channel-map
outputs.desc: Map of each information source to its capture method (quick-add, forward-to-inbox, voice memo, screenshot, clip)

outputs.name: unified-inbox-config
outputs.desc: Configuration for the single inbox where all captured items land before processing

process: List every information channel: email, Slack or chat, meetings, web browsing, reading (books, articles, PDFs), conversations, podcasts, video, social media, and your own thoughts.

For each channel, define the fastest possible capture method. The capture method must take under 10 seconds or it will not be used. Examples: email forward, share-to-app, voice memo, screenshot, browser extension clip.
Configure all capture paths to deposit into a single inbox location. Do not create separate inboxes per source. One inbox, many entry points.
Test each capture path: send a test item through each channel and verify it arrives in the inbox.

steps.description: Establish the discipline of capturing without organizing. At capture time, add only the raw material and minimal context (source, date, one tag). Never file, categorize, summarize, or decide importance at capture time.

inputs.name: capture-channel-map
inputs.desc: Map of information sources to capture methods

outputs.name: capture-protocol
outputs.desc: Written protocol for what to capture, what metadata to add, and what NOT to do at capture time

outputs.name: capture-friction-audit
outputs.desc: Audit of capture friction per channel with fixes for any path taking more than 10 seconds

process: Write the capture rule: if something is interesting, resonant, or potentially useful, capture it. Do not evaluate importance. That judgment is deferred to the organize step.
Define the minimum metadata to attach at capture time: the date (automatic), the source (where you found it), and one free-text tag (the project or topic it might relate to). Nothing else.

Write the anti-rules: do not file into folders at capture time. Do not rewrite or summarize. Do not decide if it is important. Do not spend more than 10 seconds per capture. These behaviors kill the capture habit.
Time each capture path end to end. Any path over 10 seconds gets redesigned or replaced.

steps.description: Organize captured items by active project, not by topic or category. A project is anything you are actively working on that has a deadline or a deliverable. Inactive projects get archived, not deleted.

inputs.name: capture-protocol
inputs.desc: The capture protocol defining what lands in the inbox

outputs.name: project-folder-structure
outputs.desc: The project-based folder structure with naming conventions and archival rules

outputs.name: inbox-processing-routine
outputs.desc: The routine for processing the inbox: move each item to a project folder or to the reference archive

process: List your active projects: anything with a deliverable and a timeline. These become the top-level folders. Add one folder called 'reference' for items that do not belong to a project but are worth keeping.

Define the inbox processing routine: once per day (or once per week), review each inbox item. Ask: does this relate to an active project? If yes, move it there. If no, move it to reference. If it is junk, delete it.
When a project completes, archive its folder. Do not delete. Archived projects become searchable reference material.
When a new project starts, create a folder. Pull relevant items from reference and other project archives into the new folder.

steps.description: Apply progressive summarization to items inside project folders. Layer 1: bold the key passages. Layer 2: highlight the boldest. Layer 3: write a one-sentence summary. Each pass is done only when you revisit the item, not on a schedule.

inputs.name: project-folder-structure
inputs.desc: Organized project folders with captured items

inputs.name: inbox-processing-routine
inputs.desc: The routine for moving items from inbox to projects

outputs.name: distillation-protocol
outputs.desc: The layered distillation method with rules for when to apply each layer

outputs.name: retrieval-depth-guide
outputs.desc: Guide for accessing knowledge at different depths: summary, highlights, key passages, full original

process: Layer 1 (on first revisit): bold the passages that stand out. Do not summarize. The bolding itself is the work. Takes 2 to 5 minutes per item.
Layer 2 (on second revisit): highlight the most important bolded passages. You are compressing the already-compressed version. Takes 1 to 2 minutes.
Layer 3 (on third revisit): write one sentence that captures the core idea. This is the executive summary. Takes 30 seconds.

The key discipline: each layer is applied only when you naturally revisit the item for a project. Items you never revisit never get distilled, and that is correct. The system surfaces what is useful by your own usage patterns.

steps.description: Build a search layer across all captured and organized material. Full-text search, tag search, date-range search, and project-scoped search. The search must work across all storage locations.

inputs.name: distillation-protocol
inputs.desc: The distillation method producing searchable summaries

outputs.name: search-configuration
outputs.desc: Search setup covering full-text, tag, date, and project scope across all storage

outputs.name: findability-test-results
outputs.desc: Results of testing: can you find a known item within 30 seconds using search?

process: Verify that your storage tool supports full-text search. If not, switch to one that does. Full-text search is non-negotiable because perfect organization is impossible at scale.
Tag strategy: use a flat tag list (no hierarchy). Tags are for filtering search results, not for browsing. Keep the tag count under 30; merge any tag with fewer than 5 items into a broader tag.

Test the search: pick 10 items you captured in the last month. Try to find each one in under 30 seconds using only search (no browsing folders). Any item that takes longer than 30 seconds reveals a gap in metadata or search configuration.
Set up saved searches for your active projects so you can see everything related to a project in one view.

steps.description: Design the expression step: using captured and distilled knowledge to produce something (a document, a decision, a plan, a conversation, a presentation). The system pays off here. Every expression draws from the accumulated knowledge base.

outputs.name: expression-workflow
outputs.desc: The workflow for producing outputs from the knowledge base: gather, arrange, draft, refine

outputs.name: second-brain-system-doc
outputs.desc: Complete documentation of the second brain system: capture, organize, distill, express

process: The expression workflow: when you start a new output (writing, presentation, decision, plan), begin by searching your knowledge base. Pull every relevant item into a working set.
Arrange the working set: group related items, identify gaps (what do you need that you do not have?), and sequence the ideas into a rough outline.
Draft from the working set. You are remixing and connecting existing knowledge, not starting from scratch. The value of the system is that you never start from zero.
After expression, capture any new insights that emerged during the creation process. The output feeds back into the system.

description: Build an institutional memory system with three layers: documented knowledge (procedures and how-to guides), captured decisions (decision logs with context and reasoning), and recorded expertise (expert interviews and case studies). Decisions without context become mysterious rules, so the decision layer is the most valuable.

steps.description: Audit the three knowledge layers in the organization: documented knowledge (what is written down in procedures), captured decisions (which decisions have recorded reasoning), and recorded expertise (what lives only in people's heads).

inputs.name: organization-context
inputs.desc: Description of the organization, its size, key functions, and where knowledge lives today

inputs.name: turnover-risk-areas
inputs.desc: Roles or functions where departure of a key person would cause the most damage

outputs.name: documented-knowledge-inventory
outputs.desc: List of existing documented procedures, policies, and guides with currency assessment (current, stale, missing)

outputs.name: decision-coverage-gap
outputs.desc: Assessment of which important decisions have recorded reasoning and which do not

process: Inventory all existing documentation: wikis, runbooks, SOPs, policies, onboarding guides. For each document, note the last update date and whether someone has verified its accuracy in the last 6 months.

Identify the top 20 decisions that shaped how the organization operates today. For each, check: is the reasoning recorded anywhere? Can a new person find it? Most organizations find that fewer than 5 of 20 have recorded reasoning.
Identify the top 10 people whose departure would cause the most knowledge loss. These are the knowledge holders whose expertise is not documented.
Score each area: green (documented and current), yellow (partially documented or stale), red (undocumented, lives in one person's head).

steps.description: Build the decision capture system. For each important decision, record: the question, the options considered, the chosen option, the reasoning (specific, not vague), the expected outcome, and the review date. The reasoning field is the most valuable because it is what everyone forgets.

outputs.name: decision-log-template
outputs.desc: Template for recording decisions with required fields: question, options, choice, reasoning, expected outcome, review date

outputs.name: decision-capture-trigger-list
outputs.desc: List of situations that should trigger a decision log entry (budget over X, policy change, architecture choice, hiring criteria change)

process: Design the decision record template with six fields: the question (what are we deciding?), the options (what did we consider?), the choice (what did we pick?), the reasoning (why this one and not the others?), the expected outcome (what do we expect to happen?), and the review date (when should we check if this decision was right?).

The reasoning field requires specificity. 'It seemed like the best option' is not reasoning. 'Option B had a 3-week lead time that would miss the deadline, and Option C required a skill set we do not have on the team' is reasoning.
Define the trigger list: any decision that affects budget over a threshold, changes a policy, alters system architecture, sets a hiring bar, or creates a precedent must be logged.
Retroactively capture the top 20 decisions from the audit. Interview the people who made them and record the reasoning before it is forgotten.

steps.description: Extract expertise from knowledge holders using the critical incident technique. Ask them to describe non-obvious judgment calls, not routine procedures. Document the cues they noticed, the options they considered, and what a less experienced person would have missed.

outputs.name: expert-interview-protocol
outputs.desc: Interview protocol for extracting tacit knowledge using critical incident technique

outputs.name: case-study-template
outputs.desc: Template for documenting expertise as case studies (situation, cues, judgment, outcome, lesson)

process: Identify the knowledge holders: the people others go to with questions. These are not always the most senior people. They are the people who get interrupted most often because they know things others do not.

Use the critical incident technique: ask 'Tell me about a time when you had to make a non-obvious judgment call in your work.' Follow up: 'What cues told you something was off? What options did you consider? What would a less experienced person have missed?'

Document each incident as a case study, not a procedure. Case studies preserve the context and the reasoning. Procedures strip the context away, which is exactly the part that makes expertise valuable.
Schedule one interview per week per knowledge holder. Each interview is 45 minutes. After 4 to 6 interviews per person, you have captured the bulk of their non-obvious expertise.

steps.description: Document procedures using the test-first method: write the procedure, then have someone who has never done the task follow it. Every point where they get stuck or ask a question reveals a gap in the documentation.

outputs.name: procedure-writing-guide
outputs.desc: Guide for writing procedures that pass the test-first method

outputs.name: documentation-priority-list
outputs.desc: Prioritized list of procedures to document, ordered by risk of knowledge loss

process: Write the procedure as the expert would explain it to a new person. Use numbered steps. Each step is one action. If a step contains the word 'and', split it into two steps.
Hand the procedure to someone who has never done the task. Watch them follow it without offering help. Every time they pause, ask a question, or make an error, mark that step as needing revision.
Revise the procedure to close every gap the test revealed. Then test again with a different person. Two clean runs means the procedure is ready.
Assign a freshness owner (not the author) and a review date based on how often the process changes.

steps.description: Design the retrieval system so people can find knowledge when they need it. The system must support three retrieval modes: I know what I am looking for (search), I know the topic area (browse), and I do not know what I need (guided discovery).

outputs.name: retrieval-architecture
outputs.desc: Architecture supporting search, browse, and guided discovery across all three knowledge layers

outputs.name: knowledge-navigation-map
outputs.desc: Map showing how to find decisions, procedures, and case studies from any starting point

process: Search mode: full-text search across all three layers (procedures, decisions, case studies). Tag each item with function, topic, and date so search results can be filtered.

Browse mode: organize by function (engineering, sales, operations, finance) at the top level, then by topic within each function. Each function page is a curated starting point, not a dump of all documents.
Guided discovery: for each major process, create a 'start here' page that links to the procedure, the key decisions that shaped it, and the case studies that illustrate the edge cases.
Test retrieval: give 5 different people the same question ('How do we handle X?') and see if they find the same answer. If they find different answers, the retrieval system has a gap.

steps.description: Establish the maintenance cycle that keeps institutional memory current. Stale documentation is worse than no documentation because it creates false confidence. Every document has a freshness date and an owner.

inputs.name: knowledge-navigation-map
inputs.desc: Navigation map across all knowledge layers

outputs.name: freshness-schedule
outputs.desc: Review schedule for all documentation: which documents, how often, who owns freshness

outputs.name: institutional-memory-system-doc
outputs.desc: Complete system documentation covering all three layers, capture methods, retrieval, and maintenance

process: Assign a freshness owner to every document. The owner is not necessarily the author. The owner is the person best positioned to know when the content becomes stale.
Set review cycles based on volatility: processes that change monthly get a 30-day review cycle. Stable policies get 180 days. Decisions get reviewed on their recorded review date.

The freshness review is a 5-minute check: is this still accurate? If yes, update the review date. If no, update the content or flag it for revision. If the process no longer exists, archive the document.
Track the freshness rate: what percentage of documents are within their review cycle? Below 80% means the maintenance process itself needs fixing.

description: Apply progressive summarization to any body of text. Four layers, each shorter than the last: bold the key passages, highlight the boldest, write a one-line summary, remix into your own words. The result is access to any depth of detail, from one sentence to the full original.

steps.description: Prepare the source material for progressive summarization. Ensure the full original is preserved and accessible. Add the capture metadata: source, date, and the reason you captured it.

inputs.name: source-text
inputs.desc: The original text to summarize progressively (article, notes, transcript, document)

inputs.name: capture-reason
inputs.desc: Why this material was captured (the project or question it relates to)

outputs.name: prepared-source
outputs.desc: Source material with metadata (origin, date, capture reason) preserved in its original form

outputs.name: initial-read-notes
outputs.desc: Brief notes from the first reading: what stood out, what surprised, what connects to current work

process: Preserve the full original text. Never edit, rewrite, or reorganize the original. It is the bottom layer that all other layers compress from.
Add capture metadata: the source URL or citation, the date captured, and one sentence about why you captured it.
On the first read-through, note what stands out. Do not try to be systematic. Resonance is the signal: passages that make you stop, re-read, or think 'I need to remember this' are the ones to note.
If the material is longer than 2000 words, note the sections that seem most relevant to your capture reason. You will focus your first bolding pass on those sections.

steps.description: Layer 1: bold the key passages. Read through the material and bold every passage that stands out as important, surprising, or useful. No judgment about relative importance yet. Just mark what resonates.

outputs.name: layer-one-result
outputs.desc: Source text with key passages bolded (typically 10 to 30 percent of the original)

outputs.name: bold-passage-count
outputs.desc: Number of bolded passages and the percentage of the original they represent

process: Read through the material. Bold every passage that is important, surprising, useful, or resonant. Err on the side of bolding too much rather than too little.
A bolded passage is typically 1 to 3 sentences. If you are bolding entire paragraphs, you are not compressing enough.
Target: 10 to 30 percent of the original text should be bolded. Under 10 percent means you are being too selective on the first pass. Over 30 percent means you are not compressing.
This pass should take 5 to 10 minutes for a 2000-word article. If it takes longer, you are over-thinking it.

steps.description: Layer 2: highlight the most important bolded passages. You are compressing the already-compressed version. Only the passages that capture the core ideas survive this pass.

inputs.name: bold-passage-count
inputs.desc: Count and percentage of bolded text

outputs.name: layer-two-result
outputs.desc: Source text with highlighted passages within the bolded passages (the best of the best)

outputs.name: highlight-passage-count
outputs.desc: Number of highlighted passages, typically 3 to 10 percent of the original

process: Re-read only the bolded passages. From those, highlight the ones that capture the core ideas. If you had to explain this material in 60 seconds, which bolded passages would you reference?
Target: 3 to 10 percent of the original text should be highlighted. The highlighted passages should make sense on their own when read in sequence.
This pass is done only when you revisit the material for a specific project or purpose. It is not done on a schedule.
The gap between Layer 1 and Layer 2 reveals what seemed important on first read versus what matters when you actually need the material.

steps.description: Layer 3: write a one-sentence executive summary that captures the core idea. If you can say it in one sentence, you understand it. If you cannot, go back to Layer 2.

outputs.name: executive-summary
outputs.desc: One sentence capturing the core idea of the entire source material

outputs.name: layer-three-result
outputs.desc: Complete progressive summary: one sentence, highlighted passages, bolded passages, full original

process: Read the highlighted passages. Write one sentence that captures the core idea. The sentence must be specific enough that reading it tells you whether you need to dig deeper.

Bad example: 'This article is about pricing strategies.' Good example: 'Customers anchor on the first price they see, so showing a higher-priced option first increases willingness to pay for the mid-tier option.'
If you cannot write the sentence, the highlighted passages are not capturing the core idea. Go back to Layer 2 and re-highlight.
Place the executive summary at the top of the document. The four layers are now accessible in order: summary, highlights, bold, full original.

steps.description: Layer 4 (optional): remix the material into your own words for a specific use. This is expression, not summarization. You are combining this source with your own knowledge and other sources to produce something new.

outputs.name: remixed-output
outputs.desc: The material rewritten in your own words, integrated with your existing knowledge, for a specific purpose

outputs.name: progressive-summary-complete
outputs.desc: Final artifact with all four layers accessible: remix, summary, highlights, bold, full original

process: Layer 4 is triggered by a specific need: you are writing something, making a decision, or teaching someone. You pull this material into a working set alongside other sources.
Rewrite the key ideas in your own words. Connect them to what you already know. Note where this source agrees with, contradicts, or extends other sources.
The remix is not a paraphrase. It is a synthesis: your understanding of the material applied to your specific situation.
File the remix alongside the original. You now have five levels of access: your remix, the one-sentence summary, the highlights, the bold passages, and the full original.

description: Build an information system that relies on search instead of perfect organization. Perfect organization breaks at scale because categories overlap and filing takes time. Invest in making things findable (metadata, full-text search, tags) instead of making things organized.

steps.description: Audit how much time you spend organizing versus finding information. Most people spend significant time filing and still cannot find things, which means the organization is not paying off.

inputs.name: current-information-systems
inputs.desc: Description of current file systems, note systems, email, and document management tools

inputs.name: common-retrieval-scenarios
inputs.desc: The 10 most common things you search for (recent email, a document from last month, a specific note, a meeting agenda)

outputs.name: organization-time-cost
outputs.desc: Estimated weekly time spent organizing, filing, naming, and categorizing information

outputs.name: retrieval-success-rate
outputs.desc: For each of the 10 common retrieval scenarios: how long does it take and do you find the right thing?

process: Track for one week: every time you file something (move to a folder, rename, categorize, tag), note the time spent. Sum the total.
For each of the 10 common retrieval scenarios, try to find the item right now. Time each search. Note whether you found the right version.
Calculate the ratio: time spent organizing divided by successful retrievals. If you spend 2 hours per week organizing and fail to find 3 of 10 items, the system is not working.
The question is not 'is my system organized?' but 'can I find what I need in under 30 seconds?'

steps.description: Migrate from a deep folder hierarchy to a flat or minimally structured store. Two levels maximum: a top-level category (work, personal, reference, archive) and then items. Everything within each category is flat.

inputs.name: retrieval-success-rate
inputs.desc: Retrieval success rates for common scenarios

outputs.name: flat-store-structure
outputs.desc: The new flat structure with at most two levels and clear rules for what goes where

outputs.name: migration-plan
outputs.desc: Plan for moving existing files to the flat structure without losing anything

process: Create the top-level categories. Four is usually enough: active (current projects), reference (things you look up), archive (completed work), and inbox (unsorted new items).
Within each category, items are flat. No subfolders. No sub-subfolders. If you need more structure, use naming conventions (project-name_document-type_date) instead of folders.

For the migration: do not reorganize everything at once. Move items to the flat store as you touch them. After 90 days, anything you have not touched stays in the old structure (which becomes the archive).
The discipline: when you create a new item, put it in the right top-level category and name it well. That is all the organizing you do.

steps.description: Define the metadata to add at capture time. The metadata makes items findable without requiring perfect filing. Rich metadata on a flat store beats a deep hierarchy with no metadata.

inputs.name: flat-store-structure
inputs.desc: The flat store with two levels

outputs.name: metadata-schema
outputs.desc: The metadata fields to add at capture time: date, source, project, type, and up to 3 free tags

outputs.name: tagging-discipline
outputs.desc: Rules for tagging: use existing tags first, keep the total tag count under 30, merge low-use tags quarterly

process: Required metadata at capture: date (automatic), source (where it came from), project (which active project it relates to), and type (document, note, email, image, reference).
Optional metadata: up to 3 free tags. Tags are for filtering search results, not for browsing. Use existing tags before creating new ones.
Keep the tag list under 30 total tags. More than 30 means you are over-categorizing. Every quarter, review the tag list and merge any tag with fewer than 5 items into a broader tag.
The metadata must take under 15 seconds to add. If it takes longer, you will skip it, and the system degrades.

steps.description: Invest in search capability. Configure full-text search, tag filtering, date-range search, and saved searches for common retrieval patterns. The time you save on organizing goes into making search work.

inputs.name: metadata-schema
inputs.desc: The metadata fields applied to all items

outputs.name: search-configuration
outputs.desc: Working search configuration: full-text, tag filter, date range, project scope, and saved searches

outputs.name: search-over-organize-doc
outputs.desc: Complete system documentation: flat store, metadata, search, and the quarterly maintenance routine

process: Enable full-text search across all storage. Test it: can you find a document by a phrase you remember from inside it? If not, the search tool needs to be replaced or upgraded.
Set up filtered search: search within a project, search within a date range, search by tag. These filters narrow results when full-text returns too many matches.
Create saved searches for your 10 most common retrieval scenarios. A saved search should return the answer in one click.
Run the retrieval test again: time the same 10 scenarios from the audit. Every scenario should now complete in under 30 seconds. Any that do not reveal a metadata or search gap to fix.

description: Build a decision log that makes past decisions discoverable. For each decision: the question, the options, the choice, the reasoning (specific, not vague), the expected outcome, and the review date. The reasoning field prevents relitigating the same decisions.

steps.description: Design the decision log template with six required fields. The reasoning field has the highest bar: it must be specific enough that a new person can understand why this option was chosen over the alternatives.

inputs.name: decision-context
inputs.desc: The scope of the decision log: personal, team, organization, or project

inputs.name: decision-frequency
inputs.desc: How often decisions are made that should be logged (daily, weekly, monthly)

outputs.name: decision-record-template
outputs.desc: Template with six fields: question, options, choice, reasoning, expected outcome, review date

outputs.name: reasoning-quality-standard
outputs.desc: Examples of good and bad reasoning entries to calibrate the quality bar

process: The six fields: (1) Question: what are we deciding, framed as a question. (2) Options: the alternatives considered, including 'do nothing.' (3) Choice: which option was selected. (4) Reasoning: why this option and not the others. (5) Expected outcome: what we expect to happen as a result. (6) Review date: when we should check if the decision was right.

The reasoning field standard: it must reference specific facts, constraints, or tradeoffs. 'It felt right' is not reasoning. 'Option B required 3 additional hires we do not have budget for, and Option C depended on a vendor integration that has missed two deadlines' is reasoning.
Provide three examples of good decision records and three examples of bad ones (vague reasoning, missing options, no review date) to calibrate the quality bar.
Keep the template simple. If logging a decision takes more than 10 minutes, the template is too complex and people will skip it.

steps.description: Identify which decisions deserve a log entry. Not every decision is worth logging. Define the criteria: decisions that set precedent, commit resources, are hard to reverse, or will be questioned later.

outputs.name: decision-trigger-criteria
outputs.desc: Criteria for which decisions to log: resource commitment, reversibility, precedent-setting, likely-to-be-questioned

outputs.name: decision-capture-workflow
outputs.desc: The workflow for capturing a decision: who writes it, when, where it is stored, and who reviews it

process: A decision deserves a log entry if it meets any of these criteria: it commits resources (money, people, time) above a threshold, it is hard to reverse once implemented, it sets a precedent that future decisions will follow, or it will likely be questioned by someone who was not in the room.

Define the threshold for each criterion. For a small team, the resource threshold might be one person-week of effort. For a large organization, it might be $50,000. The reversibility threshold is: could we undo this in less than a day?

Define the capture workflow: the decision maker writes the record within 24 hours of the decision. A second person reviews the reasoning field for specificity. The record is stored in a searchable, shared location.
The anti-pattern: logging too many decisions. If every small choice gets logged, the log becomes unsearchable noise. Use the trigger criteria to keep the log focused.

steps.description: Capture past decisions retroactively. Interview the people who made them and record the reasoning before it fades. Prioritize decisions that are frequently questioned or relitigated.

outputs.name: retroactive-decision-records
outputs.desc: Decision records for the most important past decisions, captured through interviews

outputs.name: relitigation-reduction-baseline
outputs.desc: Count of how often key decisions are currently questioned, to measure improvement after the log is in place

process: List the decisions that are most frequently questioned or relitigated. These are the highest-value retroactive captures because every relitigation wastes time that the log would save.

Interview the decision makers. Ask: what was the question, what options did you consider, why did you choose this one, and what do you expect to happen? If they cannot remember the reasoning, that itself is the evidence for why the log is needed.
Write the decision records and have the decision maker review them for accuracy. Store them in the log alongside new decisions.
Measure the current relitigation rate: how often per month do people question or revisit these decisions? This is the baseline. After 3 months with the log, measure again.

steps.description: Review decisions on their recorded review dates. Compare the expected outcome to the actual outcome. If the decision was wrong, record why and decide whether to reverse it. If it was right, record the evidence.

outputs.name: decision-review-process
outputs.desc: Process for reviewing decisions: compare expected vs actual outcome, record verdict, decide on action

outputs.name: decision-log-system-doc
outputs.desc: Complete decision log system documentation: template, triggers, capture workflow, review cycle, and relitigation metrics

process: On the review date, compare the expected outcome to the actual outcome. Three possible verdicts: confirmed (the decision produced the expected result), partially confirmed (some of the expected result, but not all), or reversed (the decision did not produce the expected result and should be reconsidered).

For reversed decisions: record why the decision was wrong. Was the reasoning flawed, or did circumstances change? If circumstances changed, the original decision may have been right at the time. If the reasoning was flawed, document what was missed so future decisions avoid the same error.
For confirmed decisions: record the evidence that it worked. This creates a library of decision patterns that can inform future decisions in similar situations.

Measure the improvement: compare the relitigation rate after 3 months to the baseline. A well-functioning decision log reduces relitigation by 50 percent or more, because people can look up the reasoning instead of asking or arguing.

description: Run an after-action review (AAR) that produces actionable lessons. Four questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why the difference, what will we do differently. The output must be specific actions with owners and deadlines, not vague principles.

steps.description: Define the scope of the after-action review and prepare the facts. Gather the plan (what was supposed to happen) and the actual timeline (what did happen) before the review meeting.

inputs.name: event-description
inputs.desc: Description of the event, project, or incident to review

inputs.name: original-plan
inputs.desc: The original plan, goals, or expected outcomes for the event

outputs.name: aar-scope
outputs.desc: Defined scope: what time period, what activities, and what outcomes are being reviewed

outputs.name: factual-timeline
outputs.desc: Factual timeline of what actually happened, assembled from records, logs, and participant accounts

process: Define the scope: what specific event, project phase, or incident is being reviewed? Narrow scope produces better results than broad scope. Review one sprint, not the whole project.
Assemble the factual timeline from objective sources: logs, emails, chat messages, metrics, and timelines. Get the facts straight before opinions enter the room.
Identify the participants: everyone who was involved in the event being reviewed. The AAR requires people who were there, not managers who were watching from afar.
Send the scope and factual timeline to participants 24 hours before the review so they can prepare their observations.

steps.description: Run the four-question AAR discussion. Each question builds on the last. The discipline is to stay on one question until it is answered before moving to the next.

outputs.name: aar-discussion-record
outputs.desc: Record of the four-question discussion: plan, reality, gap analysis, and proposed actions

outputs.name: gap-analysis
outputs.desc: Specific gaps between plan and reality with identified root causes

process: Question 1: What was supposed to happen? State the original plan, goals, and expected outcomes. Get agreement on what success looked like before the event. This is factual, not controversial.

Question 2: What actually happened? Walk through the factual timeline. Fill in gaps from participant accounts. The rule: no blame, no judgment, only facts. If someone says 'Bob dropped the ball,' redirect to 'What happened with the handoff to Bob?'

Question 3: Why was there a difference? This is the analysis. For each gap between plan and reality, ask why until you reach a root cause. Surface-level answers ('we ran out of time') need follow-up ('why did we run out of time? what took longer than expected? why did we underestimate?').

Question 4: What will we do differently next time? This is the output. Every answer must be a specific action, not a principle. 'Communicate better' is not an action. 'Send a status update to the channel every Friday by 4pm' is an action.

steps.description: Convert the discussion into assigned actions. Every action has an owner, a deadline, and a definition of done. Actions without owners do not get done.

outputs.name: action-register
outputs.desc: List of specific actions with owner, deadline, and definition of done

outputs.name: lesson-archive-entries
outputs.desc: Lessons formatted for the organizational lesson archive (situation, gap, root cause, action, outcome)

process: For each 'what will we do differently' answer, assign an owner. The owner is the person who can actually make the change, not the person who suggested it.
Set a deadline. If the action has no natural deadline, set one within 30 days. Actions with distant or no deadlines do not get done.
Define 'done.' How will we know this action is complete? 'Set up a weekly status update' is done when the first update is sent and the recurring calendar event exists.

Separate the actions into two categories: process changes (permanent changes to how we work) and one-time fixes (something that needs to happen once). Process changes need a verification step to confirm they stuck.

steps.description: Follow through on the actions. The value of an AAR is zero if the actions are not completed. Schedule a follow-up check 30 days after the review to verify completion.

inputs.name: action-register
inputs.desc: Actions with owners, deadlines, and done definitions

outputs.name: follow-through-report
outputs.desc: Status of each action at the 30-day check: completed, in progress, or abandoned (with reason)

outputs.name: aar-complete-record
outputs.desc: Complete AAR record: scope, timeline, discussion, actions, and follow-through results

process: Schedule the follow-up check 30 days after the AAR. Put it on the calendar at the end of the AAR meeting. If it is not scheduled, it will not happen.
At the 30-day check, review each action: completed (the thing is done and verified), in progress (underway but not done, with a new deadline), or abandoned (not going to happen, with the reason why).
For process changes, verify they are actually happening, not just set up. A weekly status update that was sent once and then forgotten is not a completed action.
Archive the complete AAR record (scope, timeline, discussion, actions, outcomes) in the institutional memory system so future teams can learn from it without running into the same problems.

description: Extract the knowledge that lives in people's heads but nowhere else. Use the critical incident technique to interview knowledge holders about non-obvious judgment calls. Document as case studies, not procedures.

steps.description: Identify the people who hold critical undocumented knowledge. They are not always the most senior people. They are the people others interrupt with questions because they know things that are not written down.

inputs.name: team-context
inputs.desc: Description of the team or organization and its key functions

inputs.name: knowledge-risk-areas
inputs.desc: Areas where losing a key person would cause the most disruption

outputs.name: knowledge-holder-map
outputs.desc: Map of knowledge holders: who holds what knowledge, how critical it is, and what would happen if they left tomorrow

outputs.name: interview-priority-list
outputs.desc: Prioritized list of who to interview first, based on knowledge criticality and departure risk

process: Ask each team: 'Who do you go to when you have a question that the documentation does not answer?' The names that come up repeatedly are the knowledge holders.
For each knowledge holder, map what they know that nobody else does. The test: if this person left tomorrow, what would break or slow down?
Assess the departure risk: are they likely to leave soon (retirement, career change, burnout)? Higher departure risk means higher extraction priority.
Rank by the product of criticality and departure risk. Interview the highest-ranked person first.

steps.description: Interview knowledge holders using the critical incident technique. Do not ask them to explain their process. Ask them to describe specific times they made a non-obvious judgment call.

outputs.name: incident-transcripts
outputs.desc: Transcripts of critical incident interviews organized by knowledge domain

outputs.name: judgment-pattern-notes
outputs.desc: Notes on recurring patterns: cues, heuristics, and rules of thumb that experts use but have never articulated

process: The opening question: 'Tell me about a time in the last year when you had to make a judgment call that a less experienced person would have gotten wrong.' Let them tell the story without interrupting.

Follow-up probes: 'What was the first thing you noticed that told you something was off?' (cues). 'What options did you consider?' (mental model). 'Why did you pick that one?' (reasoning). 'What would a less experienced person have done instead?' (expertise gap).
Do not ask 'how do you do X?' That produces procedures, not expertise. Procedures describe the happy path. Critical incidents reveal the edge cases, the exceptions, and the judgment calls.
Each interview is 45 minutes. Plan 4 to 6 interviews per knowledge holder, each covering a different domain of their expertise. Space interviews one week apart to avoid fatigue.

steps.description: Convert the interview transcripts into case studies. Each case study preserves the context, the judgment, and the reasoning. Case studies are more valuable than procedures because they preserve the 'why.'

inputs.name: incident-transcripts
inputs.desc: Interview transcripts from critical incident interviews

inputs.name: judgment-pattern-notes
inputs.desc: Notes on recurring patterns and heuristics

outputs.name: case-study-library
outputs.desc: Library of case studies organized by domain, each following the situation-cues-judgment-outcome-lesson format

outputs.name: heuristic-catalog
outputs.desc: Catalog of expert heuristics (rules of thumb) extracted from the case studies, each with the context where it applies and where it breaks down

process: Format each incident as a case study with five sections: Situation (what was happening), Cues (what the expert noticed), Judgment (what they decided and why), Outcome (what happened), and Lesson (what a less experienced person should learn from this).

From the collection of case studies, extract the heuristics: the rules of thumb that experts apply repeatedly. For each heuristic, document when it applies, when it breaks down, and what exception would override it.
Have the knowledge holder review each case study for accuracy. Their correction is itself valuable data, so note what they change and why.
Store the case studies alongside the related procedures. When someone reads the procedure for 'how to do X,' the linked case studies show 'what to do when X goes wrong in non-obvious ways.'

steps.description: Verify that the extracted knowledge actually transfers. Give the case studies and heuristics to a less experienced person and test whether they can make better judgment calls.

outputs.name: transfer-test-results
outputs.desc: Results of testing whether less experienced people make better decisions after reading the case studies and heuristics

outputs.name: tribal-knowledge-extraction-doc
outputs.desc: Complete documentation of the extraction process: identification, interview method, case study format, heuristic catalog, and transfer verification

process: Select a less experienced person in the same role. Give them a scenario from the case study library (without revealing the expert's judgment). Ask them what they would do and why.

Then give them the case studies and heuristics for that domain. Wait a week. Present a new scenario (different but in the same domain). Compare their judgment before and after the case study training.
If their judgment improves, the extraction worked. If it does not, the case studies are missing critical context. Go back to the knowledge holder and probe deeper.
The transfer test also reveals which case studies are most valuable for training. The ones that produce the biggest improvement in judgment are the ones to prioritize for new hires.

description: Design your information intake to maximize signal and minimize noise. Audit sources by signal-to-noise ratio. Cut everything below 30 percent signal. Budget time for what remains. Prioritize sources that produce actionable information over interesting-but-not-actionable content.

steps.description: Audit every information source you consume: news, email newsletters, social media feeds, Slack channels, podcasts, blogs, RSS feeds, industry reports. Score each by signal-to-noise ratio and time spent.

inputs.name: current-information-sources
inputs.desc: List of all information sources you currently consume (subscriptions, feeds, channels, newsletters, podcasts)

inputs.name: information-goals
inputs.desc: What you need information for: specific projects, ongoing education, industry awareness, personal interest

outputs.name: source-signal-scores
outputs.desc: Each source scored: signal-to-noise ratio (percentage of content that is actionable or educational), weekly time spent, and alignment with information goals

outputs.name: noise-sources-identified
outputs.desc: Sources below 30 percent signal ratio flagged for elimination

process: List every information source: email newsletters, Slack channels, social media accounts, podcasts, blogs, RSS feeds, news sites, industry reports, YouTube channels, subreddits.

For each source, review the last 10 items. Count how many were actionable (you did something because of them) or educational (you learned something you have used). Divide by 10. That is the signal ratio.
Track the time spent on each source for one week. Include both active consumption (reading, watching) and passive exposure (scrolling, notifications).
Score each source: signal ratio times relevance to your current goals. Sources that are interesting but irrelevant to current work score lower than sources that are boring but directly useful.

steps.description: Eliminate sources below the 30 percent signal threshold. Unsubscribe, unfollow, mute, or leave. The goal is not to be less informed but to be more focused on information that produces results.

inputs.name: noise-sources-identified
inputs.desc: Sources below the 30 percent signal threshold

outputs.name: eliminated-sources
outputs.desc: List of sources eliminated with the method used (unsubscribe, unfollow, mute, leave channel)

outputs.name: retained-source-list
outputs.desc: Curated list of retained sources with their signal ratios and time budgets

process: For each source below 30 percent signal: unsubscribe, unfollow, mute, or leave. Do it now, not later. Every day of delay is more noise consumed.

For sources between 30 and 50 percent signal: consider whether a filtered version exists. Example: instead of following a person on social media (30 percent signal), subscribe to their long-form blog (70 percent signal).
For sources you are reluctant to cut: schedule a 30-day trial without them. If you do not miss the information after 30 days, the source was noise disguised as necessity.
After elimination, count the total number of remaining sources. If it is more than 15, you are still consuming too broadly. Narrow further.

steps.description: Set a time budget for information consumption. Without a budget, consumption expands to fill available time. The budget forces prioritization: you can only consume X minutes per day, so you must choose the highest-signal material.

outputs.name: daily-consumption-budget
outputs.desc: Time budget for information consumption: total minutes per day, allocated across retained sources

outputs.name: consumption-schedule
outputs.desc: When to consume each source (batched, not continuous) and the cutoff rule for stopping

process: Set the total daily budget. For most people, 30 to 60 minutes of deliberate information consumption is enough. Everything beyond that is usually low-signal browsing.
Allocate the budget across retained sources. Higher-signal sources get more time. The allocation is a rough guide, not a rigid schedule.
Batch consumption into 1 to 2 time blocks per day. Do not consume information continuously. Continuous consumption fragments attention. Batched consumption is focused.
Set a cutoff rule: when the time block ends, stop. Do not 'finish one more article.' The discipline of stopping is what prevents consumption from expanding.

steps.description: Review the information diet quarterly. Sources that were high-signal six months ago may be noise now. New sources may deserve a trial. The diet is a living system, not a one-time setup.

inputs.name: consumption-schedule
inputs.desc: Current consumption schedule and cutoff rules

outputs.name: diet-review-results
outputs.desc: Quarterly review: which sources are still high-signal, which have degraded, and what new sources to trial

outputs.name: information-diet-doc
outputs.desc: Complete information diet documentation: audit method, signal scoring, elimination criteria, budget, schedule, and review cycle

process: Every quarter, re-score each retained source: review the last 10 items, count the actionable or educational ones, calculate the signal ratio. Drop any source that has fallen below 30 percent.
Check for new sources: has a colleague, mentor, or industry peer recommended something? Give it a 30-day trial. Score it after the trial.

Review the budget: is the time allocation still right? If you are consistently stopping before the budget is used, reduce the budget. If you are consistently going over, either the budget is too tight or you have too many sources.

The actionability test: from last quarter's consumption, list three specific actions you took because of something you read. If you cannot name three, the diet is too heavy on interesting and too light on useful.

description: Build a system that keeps documentation current. Every document gets a freshness date and an owner. Stale documentation is worse than no documentation because it creates false confidence.

steps.description: Inventory all documentation and score each document for staleness. A document is stale when its content no longer matches reality.

inputs.name: documentation-locations
inputs.desc: All locations where documentation lives (wikis, drives, repos, intranets, shared folders)

inputs.name: documentation-scope
inputs.desc: What categories of documentation to include (procedures, policies, technical docs, guides, FAQs)

outputs.name: document-inventory
outputs.desc: Complete inventory of documentation: title, location, last updated, subject area, current staleness score

outputs.name: staleness-assessment
outputs.desc: Percentage of documentation that is current, stale, or unknown. Stale means the content does not match current reality.

process: Inventory all documentation across all locations. For each document, record: title, location (URL or path), last modification date, and subject area.
Score staleness: a document is current if a knowledgeable person confirms it matches reality. It is stale if any part no longer matches. It is unknown if nobody has checked.
Prioritize the staleness check by usage: high-traffic documents (those people actually reference) are checked first. Documents nobody reads can wait.

Calculate the freshness rate: current documents divided by total documents. Most organizations find a freshness rate below 50 percent, which means more than half their documentation cannot be trusted.

steps.description: Assign a freshness owner to every document. The owner is not necessarily the author. The owner is the person best positioned to know when the content changes.

outputs.name: ownership-assignments
outputs.desc: Map of each document to its freshness owner, with the reasoning for each assignment

outputs.name: review-cycle-schedule
outputs.desc: Review schedule for each document based on volatility: 30 days for fast-changing topics, 90 days for moderate, 180 days for stable

process: For each document, assign the freshness owner: the person who works in the area the document covers and will notice when reality diverges from the documentation.

Set the review cycle based on volatility. Fast-changing topics (software configuration, process steps, team structure) get 30-day cycles. Moderate topics (policies, standards) get 90 days. Stable topics (legal requirements, architectural principles) get 180 days.
Cap each owner at 10 to 15 documents. More than that and the reviews will be rushed or skipped. If an owner has too many documents, split the assignment.
The owner's job is not to rewrite the document. It is to confirm 'this is still accurate' or flag 'this needs updating' and specify what changed.

steps.description: Define the review workflow: what the owner does on the review date, how to handle stale documents, and how to handle documents that should be retired.

outputs.name: review-workflow
outputs.desc: Step-by-step workflow for the freshness review: confirm, update, flag, or retire

outputs.name: stale-document-handling
outputs.desc: Policy for stale documents: mark as stale (visible warning), update within 14 days, or retire if the process no longer exists

process: On the review date, the owner reads the document and answers: is this still accurate? A 5-minute check is usually enough.

If accurate: update the review date to the next cycle and confirm. If minor edits are needed (a name changed, a URL moved): fix them now. If major rewrite is needed: flag the document for revision with a description of what changed.
Flagged documents get a visible 'under revision' banner so readers know the content may be outdated. Set a 14-day deadline for the revision.

If the process described in the document no longer exists: retire the document. Move it to an archive with a note explaining when and why it was retired. Do not delete it; someone may need the historical reference.

steps.description: Track the freshness rate over time. The rate is the percentage of documents that are within their review cycle. Below 80 percent means the maintenance system itself needs attention.

inputs.name: stale-document-handling
inputs.desc: Policy for stale and retired documents

outputs.name: freshness-dashboard
outputs.desc: Dashboard showing: overall freshness rate, freshness by owner, overdue reviews, and trend over time

outputs.name: documentation-freshness-system-doc
outputs.desc: Complete system documentation: inventory method, ownership model, review cycles, workflow, staleness handling, and tracking metrics

process: Track the freshness rate monthly: documents reviewed on time divided by documents due for review. Target is 80 percent or higher.
Break down by owner: which owners are keeping up and which are falling behind? Falling-behind owners may have too many documents, unclear ownership, or unclear review criteria.
Track the trend: is the rate improving, stable, or declining? A declining rate is an early warning that the system is losing adoption.
Review the system itself quarterly: are the review cycles right? Are the ownership assignments still correct? Are new documents being added to the system? Adjust the system, not just the documents.

description: Build a knowledge-sharing culture by embedding sharing into existing workflows. Every code review, incident, and project close generates a learning artifact. Sharing becomes a side effect of working, not a separate activity people skip when busy.

steps.description: Identify the existing workflows where knowledge is created but not captured. Every meeting, review, incident, and project close generates knowledge that evaporates unless someone writes it down.

inputs.name: team-workflows
inputs.desc: Description of the team's regular workflows: meetings, reviews, releases, incidents, project milestones

inputs.name: current-sharing-methods
inputs.desc: How knowledge is currently shared (if at all): wiki, Slack, email, word of mouth, tribal knowledge

outputs.name: sharing-opportunity-map
outputs.desc: Map of existing workflows to the knowledge they produce and whether it is currently captured or lost

outputs.name: highest-value-sharing-points
outputs.desc: Top 5 workflow points where adding a capture step would produce the most value for the least effort

process: Walk through each regular workflow: standup, code review, sprint retro, incident response, project kickoff, project close, customer call, sales demo, support ticket resolution.
For each workflow, ask: what knowledge is produced here? Who has it after the workflow completes? Is it written down anywhere? If the person who has it leaves, is the knowledge gone?
Rank the sharing opportunities by: value (how important is this knowledge?), perishability (how quickly does it become stale?), and effort to capture (how much extra work to write it down?).
Select the top 5 opportunities where the value-to-effort ratio is highest. These are the points where sharing will be embedded first.

steps.description: Design the sharing mechanism as a side effect of the existing workflow, not a separate activity. The key: the person doing the work writes the knowledge artifact as part of completing the work, not as an extra step afterward.

inputs.name: sharing-opportunity-map
inputs.desc: Workflows mapped to their knowledge production

inputs.name: highest-value-sharing-points
inputs.desc: Top 5 workflow points selected for sharing

outputs.name: sharing-mechanisms
outputs.desc: For each of the top 5 workflows: the specific sharing artifact produced, the template, and who writes it

outputs.name: definition-of-done-updates
outputs.desc: Updated definitions of done that include the sharing artifact (the work is not done until the knowledge is captured)

process: For each selected workflow, define the sharing artifact: code reviews produce a 'lessons learned' field (one sentence: what the reviewer learned), incidents produce a case study (5 sections: what happened, why, impact, fix, prevention), project closes produce a handoff document.

Embed the artifact into the definition of done. The code review is not approved until the lessons field is filled. The incident is not closed until the case study is written. The project is not complete until the handoff is filed.

Keep the artifact small. A one-sentence lesson from a code review takes 30 seconds to write. A 5-section incident case study takes 15 minutes. A handoff document takes 30 minutes. If it takes longer, the template is too complex.
Store the artifacts where people will find them: alongside the code (for code review lessons), in the incident log (for case studies), in the project archive (for handoffs).

steps.description: Roll out the sharing mechanisms. Start with one workflow, not all five. Demonstrate the value before expanding.

outputs.name: pilot-workflow-results
outputs.desc: Results from the first workflow: adoption rate, artifact quality, and time cost per person

outputs.name: rollout-plan
outputs.desc: Plan for expanding to the remaining 4 workflows, with timing and success criteria for each

process: Start with the workflow that has the highest value and the lowest effort. This is usually incident case studies or project handoffs, because the value is immediately obvious to the team.
Run the pilot for 30 days. Track: how many artifacts were created, how many workflows completed without the artifact (compliance rate), and how much time each artifact took.
After 30 days, demonstrate the value: show a situation where someone benefited from a captured artifact. One concrete example is more persuasive than any policy argument.
Expand to the next workflow only when the first one has a compliance rate above 80 percent. Expanding too fast creates resentment. Expanding after demonstrated value creates buy-in.

steps.description: Maintain the quality of shared knowledge and make it discoverable. Shared knowledge that nobody reads is a write-only database. The system must connect producers to consumers.

inputs.name: rollout-plan
inputs.desc: Plan for expanding to remaining workflows

outputs.name: quality-feedback-loop
outputs.desc: Feedback mechanism: consumers rate artifacts, producers see what was useful, quality improves over time

outputs.name: knowledge-sharing-protocol-doc
outputs.desc: Complete protocol documentation: opportunity audit, mechanism design, adoption playbook, quality loop, and discovery system

process: Build the discovery layer: a weekly digest of the most useful artifacts produced that week. This is a curated summary, not a dump. Someone selects the 3 to 5 most useful items and writes a one-line description of each.

Add a feedback mechanism: when someone reads an artifact and finds it useful (or useless), they can mark it. Over time, this feedback identifies the highest-quality producers and the most useful formats.

Review artifact quality quarterly: sample 10 artifacts from each workflow. Are they specific enough to be useful? Are they too brief to convey the lesson? Adjust the templates based on what is working.

The ultimate metric: time-to-competence for new hires. If the shared knowledge base is working, new people ramp up faster because they have access to the judgment, decisions, and lessons that used to live only in long-tenured people's heads.
